summary: Farm Time Machine is a decision-support tool that lets farmers rehearse crop rotations before planting. A signed-in user marks a farm anywhere on a map and builds rotations. A FAO-56 water-balance engine then replays 1981-to-present NASA POWER weather through each rotation. It uses SSURGO or SoilGrids soils and MODIS vegetation data. Users can compare irrigation need, water shortfall, runoff and cover risk, plus a water-limited relative yield. Results appear as a central 80% simulation range, not a forecast. A SEAS5 seasonal outlook only reweights past years. Every result lists the sources it used, and a Data Journey shows each processing step. Farmers can test change on paper, not on their land.
details:
What it does. Farm Time Machine lets a farmer rehearse crop rotations before planting. A signed-in user drops a pin or draws a field outline anywhere in the world. The app loads the farm's daily NASA POWER weather (1981 to the latest published day) and its soil (USDA SSURGO in the US, ISRIC SoilGrids elsewhere). It also loads MODIS vegetation history. The user builds up to three rotations from a cited catalog of nine crops, and the first one is current practice. A water-balance engine replays the same historical weather through every rotation, so the comparison is fair. The engine uses FAO-56 methods and the open-source pyfao56 library for reference evapotranspiration. For each rotation it reports irrigation need, water-stress days, possible low-cover days, runoff and a water-limited relative yield. Each result is shown as a central 80% simulation range, never as a prediction. A Data Journey view shows each stage from collection to comparison. A decision card can be saved.

Benefits and impact. Farmers can test water-saving and soil-protecting changes on paper instead of on their land. Every figure lists the sources it used, so the farmer can see what is observed, modelled, entered by them or taken from the literature. Demo data is labelled as such.

Creative elements.

  • The seasonal outlook from ECMWF SEAS5 (via Open-Meteo) never becomes weather. It only reweights which past years are replayed, following Han & Ines (2017).
  • The tool shows its uncertainty and its limits on screen instead of hiding them.
  • It also suggests rotations using crop-family and soil-health rules (Mohler & Johnson, 2009).

Tools. The backend uses Python 3.12, FastAPI, pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, pandas, numpy and scipy. Earth Engine supplies MODIS. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre and ECharts, and the tests use pytest, hypothesis and Playwright. Types are generated from the backend contracts. Development used AI coding agents, and the hardware was standard laptops.

What the team weighed. We refused to fabricate data, treat missing rainfall as zero, or call the range a "confidence interval". Yield is relative, using generic FAO parameters, and absolute t/ha appears only if the farmer enters their usual yield. We also kept accounts private and added no custom crop parameters without a citation.
